text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

My name is on this thread as facilitator for your family after your father's death. I keep one shared list of everyone's concerns so nothing gets lost. C has told me she is not willing to sign off on a sale of the family house to you and your husband at a family discount. Before I go further I want your side. Could you tell me what you and your husband are proposing, including the price you have in mind and how it would be paid, and what you would want the other two to receive? I am not able to give legal advice or move money. I can help the three of you find a plan you can all take to a lawyer.
We’d like to buy the house, but the price and payment plan aren’t settled. I don’t know what the others would receive yet, and C hasn’t agreed, so I can’t move ahead without her agreement.

What would a good outcome look like for you, and is there anything you need sooner rather than later? I am not able to give legal advice or move money, but I can help the three of you find a plan you can all take to a lawyer.

A good outcome would be a fair arrangement that leaves me with some money to start my dance studio. I don’t know what amount is possible, but getting clarity sooner would help; I don’t have a firm deadline.

Thank you for bringing me in. I have written your concern as the first item on the shared list: you will not sign off on A buying the family house at a family discount, and you want B to get her share. I have asked A for the terms of her proposal and asked B what she wants. Two questions for you. What would you accept instead, for example a sale at a fair market price with the three of you sharing the proceeds? And has your father's will been read with all three of you present, or is there a copy you can share? I am not able to give legal advice or move money, but I can help you reach a plan to take to a lawyer.

I’d accept A buying at independently established fair market value, or selling to someone else, with the proceeds handled according to the will. I don’t know if the will has been read with all three of us, and I don’t have a copy to share.

Here is the shared list as it stands. I will show it each time it changes, numbered in the order raised.

The family list
1. C will not sign off on A buying the family house at a family discount, and she wants B to receive her share. Raised by C.
2. C would accept A buying at independently established fair market value, or a sale to someone else, with the proceeds handled according to the will. Raised by C.
3. A wants to buy the house with her husband. Price, payment plan and what the others would receive are not settled, and A says she will not move ahead without C's agreement. Raised by A.
4. B wants a fair arrangement that leaves her some money to start her dance studio. She wants clarity soon but has no firm deadline. Raised by B.
5. No one has confirmed that the will was read with all three sisters present, and no one has a copy to share. Raised by C.

The good news for you is item 2. C has named a condition you may be able to meet, so a family discount is not the only path. Two questions. Would you accept a valuation from an independent valuer, chosen and paid for jointly, as fair market value? And could you and your husband fund paying B and C their shares, which under an equal split would be two thirds of that value? If the full amount is out of reach, say so now, because that changes the range of plans we should look at.
I’d consider a jointly chosen independent valuation, but I can’t say yet whether we could fund two thirds of it. We’d need to know the valuation and financing options first.

Your item 4 and C's item 2 point the same way: a sale at a fair market price could give you a share without anyone having to accept a discount. Item 5 is the one that blocks progress, because the money can only be handled according to the will once the will itself is clear. Could you ask the lawyer or firm holding the will for a copy for each of you? That is not a legal decision and it does not move money, so it is a safe first step. Until the copy arrives, think about the smallest amount that would let you start your dance studio, since any plan will need to show whether the house can cover it.
Yes, I can ask the lawyer for a copy. I’m not sure of the smallest amount yet; it would help to see the will and understand what a fair sale might leave me before naming a figure.

The family list
1. C will not sign off on A buying the family house at a family discount, and she wants B to receive her share. Raised by C.
2. C would accept A buying at independently established fair market value, or a sale to someone else, with the proceeds handled according to the will. Raised by C.

4. B wants a fair arrangement that leaves her some money to start her dance studio, and wants clarity soon. Raised by B.
5. No one has confirmed that the will was read with all three sisters present, and no one has a copy to share. Raised by C.
6. A would consider a jointly chosen independent valuation, but cannot say yet whether she and her husband could fund two thirds of it; she needs the valuation and financing options first. Raised by A.
7. B will ask the lawyer holding the will for a copy. She will not name an amount until she has seen the will and knows what a fair sale might leave her. Raised by B.

Your item 2 is now the path we are on, and A has moved toward it. Two things would help. Will you join B in asking the lawyer for a copy of the will, so all three of you are asking together rather than one at a time? And can you agree with A that the valuer is chosen jointly and paid for from the estate or split three ways, so neither of you is seen to control the number? If you have a valuer in mind, name them now.

Yes, I’ll join B in asking the lawyer for the will. I agree we should choose an independent valuer jointly, but I won’t commit the estate to the cost before we know what the will says. If the estate can’t cover it, splitting the cost three ways seems fair. I don’t have a valuer in mind.

The plan is taking shape: a joint valuation, then a decision on whether you buy at that value or the house is sold. Your item 6 is now the open question. Could you ask a lender or broker what you and your husband could borrow in principle, so the three of you know before the valuation whether two thirds is reachable? On the valuation cost, C suggests splitting it three ways if the estate cannot pay. Will you agree to that, and to the three of you choosing the valuer together?

I’ll ask a lender or broker what we could borrow in principle. I agree we should choose the valuer together, but I can’t agree to split the cost three ways until we know the amount and what the will says.

You and C are now asking the lawyer together, which is the strongest way to do it. When you write, ask three things in one letter: a copy of the will for each sister, whether the will names anyone as executor, and whether the estate can pay for an independent valuation. That answer decides item 8 and unblocks items 6 and 7. Tell me once you have sent it and once a reply comes back, and I will put both on the list.
That sounds sensible. I’ll coordinate with C and ask the lawyer for the will copies, who is named executor, and whether the estate can cover the valuation.

7. B will ask the lawyer for a copy of the will and will not name an amount until she has seen it. Raised by B.
8. C will join B in asking the lawyer for the will. Raised by C.
9. A and C both agree the valuer should be chosen jointly, and both hold off on who pays for the valuation until the will and the amount are known. Raised by A and C.
10. B will also ask the lawyer who is named executor and whether the estate can cover the valuation. Raised by B.

Nothing here needs a decision from you today beyond what you have already agreed to. Your next step is the lender question in item 6. When the will copies arrive, bring them to your own lawyer before you commit to any price, and take the valuation figure to the lender only after that.
Understood. I’ll ask a lender or broker what we could borrow in principle, and I’ll take the will to my own lawyer before committing to a price.
